newsitem.title: USA: Mass. proposes tax cut, rise in "rainy day" cap.
newsitem.headline: Mass. proposes tax cut, rise in "rainy day" cap.

text.p: Massachusetts' legislators and governor Monday proposed using budgeted tax revenues instead of current tax revenues as the basis for calculating the 5.0 percent take for the state's "rainy day" fund cap.
The change would mean the "rainy day" fund's cap would have risen to $866 million in fiscal 1996 from $543 million, the officials said at a Beacon Hill press conference.

The legislators also said personal income taxes would be cut this year, as mandated by a 1986 law that requires any funds exceeding the rainy day cap to be returned to taxpayers. The cut will come into effect in April and total $85 million.
"In plain English, our 'rainy day' fund is saturated and the revenue overspill will flow back to its rightful owners -- the people of Massachusetts," Gov. William Weld told reporters.

Weld said changing the method used to calculate the "rainy day" or state's stabilization fund, a pool of money set aside to be used in hard economic times, "should also be good news for our bond rating."
Weld said only one other state, Virginia, uses tax revenues as the basis for its stabilization fund.
However, Moody's Investors Service rates Massachusetts general obligation debt as A1, while Standard & Poor's Corp rates the Commonwealth's debt A-plus. Both rate Virginia a triple-A.
In effect, the change in calculating the "rainy day" cap will automatically put more cash in state coffers, as budgeted tax revenues generally exceed tax revenues.

The "rainy day" fund is used to cover shortfalls in revenues during years of economic downturn. In those periods, working the cap off a presumably higher level of revenues will tide the state over rough times.
Democratic legislative leaders flanked the Republican Weld at the statehouse press conference. Senate President Thomas Birmingham said raising the cap was the prudent thing to do.
"In these relatively good economic times we have to prepare for the inevitable downturn," Birmingham said.
"Increasing the capacity of the stabilization fund strengthens governments ability to fulfill its basic responsibility in tough times when its resources may be most valued."
